title: Live Human Feedback in the Training Loop: Aligning Diffusion Models with Real People
gist: Rapidata argues online RLHF for diffusion and video models should replace learned reward models (PickScore, ImageReward), which drift and get reward-hacked, with live crowd feedback via its Flows API plugged into Flow-GRPO. It sizes the load at about 2,400 human responses per minute for a 24-GPU run and claims sub-minute turnaround.

themes.theme: Reward-model proxies as the weak link in visual RLHF

insights.claim: Online RL methods like Flow-GRPO outperform offline preference optimization such as Diffusion-DPO and Flow-DPO, mirroring findings for LLM preference fine-tuning, because offline feedback distributions stay fixed while the policy changes.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: On-policy feedback is the established direction for image/video post-training, so the open question is the quality of the signal, not the method.
insights.quote: Methods that directly optimize on human preferences, such as Diffusion-DPO [5], generally collect them offline, before optimization begins, meaning that the feedback distribution remains fixed as the policy changes.

insights.claim: Learned reward models such as PickScore and ImageReward can diverge from human judgement when the output distribution shifts away from their training data, and are exploitable via reward hacking.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Proxy reward quality caps the ceiling of online RLHF for generative media; a human-in-loop signal is the claimed fix.
insights.quote: These proxies can diverge from human judgement, especially when the output distribution shifts away from the reward model's training data, and they may be exploited during optimization (reward hacking)

insights.claim: Documented reward-hacking failure modes include collapsed visual diversity and artifact-prone images that still score highly; curated image pairs with obvious glitches receive similar scores from common reward models.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Evidence that automated scorers are blind to glitches suggests quality gains from RL on proxies may be overstated.
insights.quote: for example by collapsing visual diversity [7] or by producing artifact-prone images that still score highly [10]

insights.claim: Human preference alignment is now a standard step across image, video and even world models; without it outputs are less pleasing, natural and coherent.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Alignment data and feedback is a recurring, scaling demand across all visual generative stacks, creating a market for annotation infrastructure.
insights.quote: Human preference alignment is a crucial step in the training process of most visual generative models, be it image-, video-, or, more recently, even world models [1,2,3,4].

themes.theme: Real-time human feedback as a new post-training paradigm

insights.claim: The obvious fix of using real humans as the training signal is bottlenecked by latency: massive preference data must arrive fast enough to avoid expensive idle GPU compute.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: The constraint shifts from annotation cost to annotation latency; whoever solves turnaround time owns the niche.
insights.quote: speed and latency become a huge factor, since you need to collect a lot of preference data in a very short amount of time to keep up with the training loop and avoid extensive (and expensive) idle compute time.

insights.claim: Rapidata claims its setup enables a completely new paradigm of post-training for visual generative models by plugging human ratings in place of the reward model, and says it has been used for large-scale model training.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Vendor claim without named customers or results in this post; treat as marketing until benchmarks appear.
insights.quote: At Rapidata, we have built a setup that supports exactly that, enabling a completely new paradigm for post-training of visual generative models.

insights.claim: In Flow-GRPO the human feedback slots in at the grading step (step 2), replacing only the reward model while advantage calculation and weight updates stay unchanged, so integration is a drop-in swap.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Low switching cost for labs already running GRPO-style loops, which lowers adoption friction for human-feedback vendors.
insights.quote: Rapidata's API slots in seamlessly at step 2 to replace the reward model. Everything else can be kept the same.

insights.claim: The approach is claimed to adapt to other algorithms including AdvantageFlow, Advantage Weighted Matching and Pref-GRPO, which works with pairwise preferences directly.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Algorithm-agnostic positioning broadens addressable customers, though only Flow-GRPO is walked through.

insights.claim: Rapidata Flows decompose group ranking into pairwise comparisons by a crowd, aggregate them via the Bradley-Terry model into Elo-style scores per image, and normalize within each group to get advantages, so the absolute Elo scale does not matter.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: A 1952 paired-comparison statistic is the mechanism turning crowd clicks into RL rewards.
insights.quote: Because the scores are normalized within each group, the absolute Elo scale does not matter.

insights.claim: Hundreds of groups are rated asynchronously in parallel, and rating can start before a whole batch is generated, which minimizes GPU idle time.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Pipelined human evaluation is what makes the loop economically feasible.
insights.quote: Note that the potentially hundreds of different groups are rated asynchronously in parallel

themes.theme: Throughput economics and scaling of human feedback

insights.claim: Required human feedback bandwidth scales proportionally with compute: the more images generated, the more feedback needed.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Human-feedback demand becomes a function of GPU fleet size, tying annotation vendors' revenue to training compute growth.
insights.quote: The human feedback bandwidth you need is proportional to your compute: the more images you generate, the more feedback you need.

insights.claim: For the Flow-GRPO setup (24 A800 GPUs, 48 groups of 24 images per step), Rapidata estimates 100-150 responses per group and a 3-minute deadline, implying about 2,400 feedback responses per minute (48 x 150 / 3).
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete sizing: roughly 2.4k human judgements per minute for a modest 24-GPU run, scaling linearly for frontier clusters.
insights.quote: that results in a feedback bandwidth of 2,400 responses per minute

insights.claim: Rapidata says it can consistently return ratings on sub-minute deadlines, and the remaining idle time can be removed by shifting evaluation one step so feedback on one batch is collected while the next is generated.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Asynchronous off-by-one scheduling trades slight staleness for full GPU utilization.
insights.quote: While the system is extremely fast and can consistently return ratings on sub-minute deadlines

insights.claim: Full-model updates during alignment are uncommon and often undesirable; training a LoRA is the more efficient approach.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Alignment loops are lightweight adapters, which makes frequent human-in-loop iteration cheaper.
insights.quote: Updating the entire model during alignment post-training is uncommon and often undesirable.

insights.claim: At scale, hundreds or thousands of GPU workers each authenticating can trigger bursts of token refreshes and rate limiting; the recommended fix is a single coordinator that authenticates and shares a token file.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Shows human-in-loop RLHF is an operational distributed-systems problem, with credential handling as a risk surface.
insights.quote: authenticate once in a coordinator process (e.g. rank 0) and share the token.

insights.claim: Rapidata offers programmatic access to a massive crowd of annotators for short-form tasks, with Flows as the feature built specifically for real-time online RLHF; advanced tuning such as response counts per group needs vendor assistance.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: The product is partly service-led, with consulting touchpoints likely a revenue and lock-in lever.
insights.quote: Rapidata provides programmatic access to a massive crowd of annotators for short-form tasks

insights.claim: Rapidata offers research grants of annotation credits to academic projects aligned with online RLHF, a funnel to seed benchmarks and papers that validate the real-human-feedback approach.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: Academic credits are a cheap way to generate citations and evidence for the paradigm.
insights.quote: you may also qualify for our research grants, which provide annotation credits for projects with topics aligned to our own research, such as online RLHF.

insights.claim: The core pitch: removing the proxy reward model keeps the feedback signal aligned with what people actually prefer even as the model's output distribution shifts during training.
insights.speaker: Mads Kuhlmann-Joergensen
insights.so_what: If true, human-in-loop signals become the defensible quality differentiator for image/video models as proxy scorers saturate.
insights.quote: Online RLHF with real human feedback removes the need for a proxy reward model and keeps the feedback signal aligned with what people actually prefer
